signal.title: [Spec][Ngram] 7/N: Dynamically select draft token counts from SAMs and Trie
signal.text: <!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. --> ## Motivation <!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. --> Part of Ngram series https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21052 This PR removes the old fixed trie/SAM draft-budget split. Instead of reserving draft tokens with `external_sam_budget`, trie and each loaded SAM are treated as candidate sources scored by `score = source_prior * (w_specificity * specificity + w_confidence * confidence)` where `w_specificity` and `w_confidence` are normalized from the user-provided weights. Sources are merged in score order, and the final merged tree is capped only by `num_draft_tokens`. This lets multiple external corpora participate in drafting without hard partitioning draft capacity across trie and SAMs. Followed by https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/22569 which benchmarks this PR's effect on accept length across some experiments ## Modifications <!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. --> - Add C++ external-corpus SAM support for Ngram, including suffix automaton matching, root-result merging, and multi-corpus management. - Wire the feature through FFI / Python / worker plumbing so external corpora can be loaded and used during Ngram speculative decoding. - Replace static trie/SAM budget allocation with score-ordered source merging. Remove `external_sam_budget` and `min_trie_share`; keep `trie_source_prior`, `match_specificity_weight`, and `match_confidence_weight` as source-ranking knobs. - Update unit/spec coverage for external corpus loading, multi-SAM merge behavior, server args, and the output-as-corpus accept-length regression. - signal.title: Support Structured Outputs with enable_thinking=False in Qwen3
signal.text: ## Motivation Resolves https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/6675 The current `ReasoningGrammarBackend` doesn't support generation with `enable_thinking=False`. signal.title: [Kernel] DSv4 top-k v2: raw_indices output + adaptive cluster split
signal.text: Route raw_indices callers through v2 instead of the ~2x slower v1, and add an adaptive small-batch cluster split factor N in {8,4,2} chosen from (batch, max_seq_len) so mid-batch long-context launches stay a single cluster-wave. Split caps are B200/sm100 autotune values scaled by SM count at runtime; shapes outside the split bands fall back unchanged. topk_impl.cuh is untouched (TopKCluster<N> was already generalized to any power-of-two N). Correctness validated against torch.topk at zero tolerance for both the page-transformed and raw outputs: test_topk_v2.py 296 passed (244 existing + 52 new split-band cases). Perf on B200: win region 0.62-0.92x (best ~1.6x), fallback/short-seq within noise, page-only neutral. <!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. --> ## Motivation `topk_transform_512_v2` is the DeepSeek-V4 DSA-indexer fused top-k: it selects the per-row top-k of `scores` (ragged `seq_lens`) and writes the page-table transform of the selected indices. Two limitations remain: 1. **The raw (pre-transform) index output is gated off in the indexer.** v2 is only used when `raw_indices is None`; any caller that also needs the raw selected positions falls back to v1 (`topk_transform_512`), which is markedly slower on long context. v2 already carries a `raw_out` pointer — it was simply not wired up on the raw-needing path. 2. **The small-batch cluster path leaves SMs idle on mid-batch long rows.** The fused small-batch kernel splits one row across a fixed 8-block cluster. An N-block cluster must be co-resident (DSMEM), so an 8-way split only stays a single cluster wave up to a batch proportional to `SM_count / 8`. Above that, mid-batch long-context launches either spill into a second wave or fall back to the persistent pool + streaming `main<3>`, both of which run the long rows over serial waves while most SMs sit idle (achieved occupancy ~50%). <!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. --> ## Modifications Two behavioral files plus one runtime helper; `topk_impl.cuh` is untouched. ### `indexer.py` — route `raw_indices` through v2 ```diff -elif envs.SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2.get() and raw_indices is None: +elif envs.SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2.get(): topk_transform_512_v2( - ..., indexer_metadata.topk_metadata, + ..., indexer_metadata.topk_metadata, raw_indices, ) ``` `topk_transform_512_v2`'s signature already ends in `out_raw_indices: Optional`, so raw-needing callers stay on v2 instead of dropping to v1. `raw_indices is None` produces the identical page-only behavior as before. ### `topk_v2.cuh` — adaptive cluster-split factor N ∈ {8, 4, 2} `topk_small_batch_kernel` is templated on the split factor: ```cpp template <bool kPDL, uint32_t kNumRanks = kClusterSize> TOPK_KERNEL __cluster_dims__(1, kNumRanks, 1) void topk_small_batch_kernel(...) ``` The body uses `ClusterT = impl::TopKCluster<kNumRanks>` and `worker_rank = blockIdx.x % kNumRanks`; the epilogue and synchronization are otherwise unchanged. `TopKCluster<N>` is already generalized to any power-of-two N, so `topk_impl.cuh` needs no change and N ∈ {2, 4} reuse the existing implementation. The host selects N from `(batch_size, max_seq_len)` so the split stays a single cluster wave, and falls back unchanged otherwise: - **8-way** (large seq, small batch) — the original small-batch path. - **4-way** — mid-batch band above the 8-way cap. - **2-way** — lowest coordination cost (2-rank DSMEM all-reduce); the band above the 4-way cap and a lower seq floor. - **else** — persistent pool + `main<3>`, identical to the current code, so no shape outside the split bands is perturbed. Each split is bounded by a **batch cap** and a **seq floor**. Both are derived from hardware and rescaled to the running device at launch: - **Batch cap** scales with SM count (an N-block cluster must be co-resident, so the single-wave batch ceiling is proportional to the SM count). - **Seq floor** scales with L2 cache size. The kernel scans each row twice (a radix pass to fix the threshold, then a gather pass); while a row fits in L2 the second pass is an L2 re-read, but once it spills, the second pass re-reads from DRAM and a single streaming block becomes bandwidth-bound — which is where the split begins to pay off. Thresholds are calibrated on sm_100 (152 SMs, 128 MB L2) and kept as kernel-side `constexpr` anchors; the runtime scaling reproduces those values exactly on sm_100 and routes by each device's own SM count and L2 size elsewhere, with clamps so a smaller device cannot scale a cap below its neighbouring band or a seq floor at/under the cluster floor. Routing only affects which path a shape takes — every path computes the same top-k, so device scaling cannot change results, only performance. This adds `host::runtime::get_l2_cache_size` in `runtime.cuh` alongside the existing `get_sm_count`. <!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. --> ## Accuracy Tests Validated against `torch.topk` (largest, per-row over `scores[i, :seq_len]`) with **zero tolerance**: per-row top-k index-set equality plus matching `-1` padding, for both the page-transformed output and the raw index output. The existing `MAX_PERMIT_ERROR = 5` only forgives fp16-histogram equal-score tie swaps and is unchanged. `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_topk_v2.py`: **296 passed** on B200 (244 existing + 52 new). The new `test_topk_v2_split` covers the 8/4/2-way bands, each split's batch cap, the low-seq 2-way band, and the persistent-pool fallback (batch/seq just outside every band), × k ∈ {512, 2048} × identity/perm page tables, checking both the transformed and raw outputs against `torch.topk`. Correctness is routing-independent, so these cases validate every split factor regardless of which one a given device's scaled thresholds select. <!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. --> ## Speed Tests and Profiling CUDA-event median on B200 (sm_100); ratio = this PR / current v2, so **< 1 is faster**. raw-index path (page-only tracks it): | batch | seq | ratio | note | |------:|-------:|:-----:|:-----| | 76 | 262144 | **0.62** | ~1.6× | | 75 | 262144 | 0.73 | | | 48 | 114688 | 0.74 | | | 48 | 131072 | 0.76 | | | 72 | 262144 | 0.77 | | | 74 | 262144 | 0.78 | | | 72 | 196608 | 0.81 | | | 64 | 262144 | 0.92 | | | 76 | 262144 | 0.62 | k=2048 | Shapes outside the split bands (larger batch, short sequences) are dispatched identically to the current code and stay within `0.95–1.02×` run-to-run noise. NCU confirms the mechanism: a single split kernel in one cluster wave replaces the baseline's persistent-pool multi-wave + `main<3>` chain. signal.text: ## Motivation Support prefix cache for Qwen3.5 on Ascend NPU. When serving Qwen3.5 with the Ascend attention backend, the NPU backend defaults `page_size` to 128. signal.title: fix: propagate rank-local tensor update failures
signal.text: ## Motivation `update_weights_from_tensor` currently runs a rank-local update and then enters a plain TP CPU/Gloo barrier. If one rank raises during the local update (or during its requested cache flush), that rank exits the handler while its peers wait in the barrier until the process-group timeout. The original rank-local exception is also lost from the peer-visible response. We observed this failure mode on TP=8 with EAGLE v2: TP0 remained in the CUDA-IPC tensor unwrap/update path, while TP1-7 timed out after 7200000 ms in the final Gloo barrier. This is separate from, but can amplify, the EAGLE CUDA-IPC handle issue tracked in #17870. ## Changes - Convert rank-local tensor update and cache-flush exceptions into a failure status. - Use `all_gather_object` as the terminal TP synchronization point. - Aggregate failures with their TP rank so the initiating caller sees the first useful error instead of a later barrier timeout. - Preserve local cache cleanup before aggregating peer failures, because a locally successful rank may already have changed weights even if another rank failed. - Remove the redundant plain barrier after the status gather. - Add CPU unit coverage for peer failures, local exceptions, cache-flush failures, and TP=1 success. ## Scope This does not recover a process that is already dead or a rank stuck forever inside a model-loader/CUDA operation. It prevents ordinary rank-local Python failures from stranding peers and makes the failure diagnosable. ## Test plan - `git diff --check` - `python -m py_compile` on the modified implementation and test - Lightweight mocked-module execution verified that a peer failure is returned on all ranks and the terminal status gather is reached. - Full upstream unit CI requested for `test_weight_updater_rank_failures.py`. <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31996872749](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31996872749)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31996872588](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31996872588)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.author: polisettyvarma

signal.title: [Fix] Account resident weight memory in KV sizing
signal.text: ## Motivation The IPC weight-cache daemon keeps model weights resident before the engine starts, so `ModelRunner` samples its pre-load free-memory baseline after those weights have already reduced free memory. Without correcting that baseline, KV sizing reserves headroom from only the remaining free memory and can over-allocate the KV cache. The correction must be rank-local before the distributed `MIN`: adding preloaded weight memory after ranks have already reduced their baselines is incorrect when rank footprints differ. Target KV sizing also happens after draft loading, so target, multi-runner, and future speculative draft weights must be aggregated before sizing. ## Modifications - Add a generic rank-local `BaseModelLoader.preloaded_weights_bytes` contract, defaulting to zero, and validate loader-provided values before use. - Aggregate preloaded bytes across target, multi-runner, and speculative draft workers. The current built-in IPC weight cache plus speculative decoding combination remains explicitly rejected because draft-model daemon support is not implemented yet, but the accounting path is ready for it. - Immediately before target KV-pool allocation, compute `MIN(local pre-load baseline + local preloaded weight bytes)` and update `pre_model_load_memory`, so initial sizing and post-capture resizing use the same corrected value. - Measure the daemon's process-local PyTorch allocator growth during model loading and return it through the IPC protocol as `preloaded_weights_bytes`. ## Accuracy Tests Ran a real persistent-daemon restart A/B with `Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct` in BF16 at TP=1 on an 80 GB GPU. The standalone daemon retained 63,004 MiB of GPU memory while two independent engine clients were started sequentially against the same daemon. | Result | Without this fix | With this fix | |---|---:|---:| | Client pre-load available memory | 17.23 GB | 17.23 GB | | Reported preloaded weights | Not available | 65,546,485,760 bytes (61.045 GiB) | | KV cache tokens | 63,434 | 38,430 | | K + V allocation | 15.48 GB | 9.38 GB | | Memory before decode graph capture | 0.88 GB | 4.37 GB | | First client start | CUDA OOM during graph capture | Healthy; inference succeeded | | Second client start | Same CUDA OOM | Healthy; inference succeeded | Without the correction, both starts selected the same oversized KV cache and failed during decode CUDA graph capture while the daemon remained alive. With the correction, both starts completed graph capture, reached health, and served a completion against the same persistent daemon. This validates the final implementation and reproduces the accounting defect as a deterministic startup failure with a model whose resident weights occupy more than half of GPU memory. ## Speed Tests and Profiling Not benchmarked. The steady-state inference path is unchanged. Startup adds two process-local allocator reads and one existing-world-group reduction before KV-pool allocation. ## Validation - Large-model persistent-daemon restart A/B passed as described above - Python syntax checks passed for all changed production files - Ruff error checks passed for all changed production files - Full Ruff checks passed for the central accounting and IPC modules - Diff whitespace checks passed ## Checklist - [x] Format code according to the repository hooks. - [x] Validate the exact final implementation with a persistent GPU daemon and two engine starts. - [ ] Update documentation — not applicable; no user-facing option or workflow changed. <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31773025443](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31773025443)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31773025113](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31773025113)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: Fix Description for MTP Model update_weights_from_tensor API OOM Issue
signal.text: ## Problem Background Multiple calls to the MTP model's `update_weights_from_tensor` API for parameter updates will result in **OOM due to memory leakage**. ### Root Cause Analysis: 1. SGLang and the RL engine communicate via **inter-process communication (IPC)**, with parameters transmitted through **CUDA IPC**. 2. In `EAGLEWorker/EAGLEWorker2`, `update_weights_from_tensor` sequentially invokes: - `draft_worker.draft_runner.update_weights_from_tensor()` - `target_worker.model_runner.update_weights_from_tensor()` 3. **Each worker deserializes the** `named_tensors` **independently**, causing the CUDA IPC handle in `LocalSerializedTensor` to be opened twice (via `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle`) but closed only once (via `cudaIpcCloseMemHandle`), leading to memory leakage. ## Solution Add a new `unwrap_ipc_tensors` function to perform IPC allocation and deallocation **only once per update process**. ### Function Implementation ```python def unwrap_ipc_tensors( named_tensors: List[Tuple[str, torch.Tensor]], tp_rank: int, device: torch.device ) -> List[Tuple[str, torch.Tensor]]: """Unwrap LocalSerializedTensor objects to detach from IPC memory. This function should be called only once after deserialization to avoid opening multiple CUDA IPC handles for the same tensor. """ result = [] for name, tensor in named_tensors: if isinstance(tensor, LocalSerializedTensor): ipc_tensor = tensor.get(tp_rank) result.append((name, ipc_tensor.to(device))) del ipc_tensor else: result.append((name, tensor.to(device))) return result ``` ## Modified Files 1. **`python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner.py`**: Add the `unwrap_ipc_tensors` function. 2. **`eagle_worker.py/eagle_worker_v2.py`**: In `update_weights_from_tensor`, **prioritize** the deallocation logic for deserialized IPC tensors, and unwrap the tensors before passing them to the two workers. This ensures that each IPC handle of `LocalSerializedTensor` is opened and closed exactly once, preventing OOM issues caused by memory leakage. ## Accuracy Tests <!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. --> ## Benchmarking and Profiling <!-- If this pull request impacts inference speed, provide benchmarking and profiling results. --> ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review Process 1. signal.title: [Scheduler] Reuse per-step cuda events uniformly (WAR read_done + copy_done)
signal.text: ## Motivation Follow-up to #31468, several paths construct a fresh cuda `Event()` every decode step: the WAR `read_done` in `DecodeCudaGraphRunner.execute()` (twice per DFlash step: draft + verify runners), the same in `EagleDraftExtendCudaGraphRunner`, and the scheduler's `copy_done` (both the overlap and non-overlap spec paths). Each costs a `cudaEventCreate` + Python object churn (~µs/step) — not a host sync, purely allocation/GC hygiene, so no throughput change is expected; a no-regression A/B is attached below. ## Modifications - New `ReusableEventRing` (`sglang/srt/utils/cuda_event_ring.py`): lazy fixed ring of re-recordable events; a slot is re-recorded only after every consumer of its previous record has waited/synchronized, so depth = max records in flight (+ margin). - `read_done` sites (decode graph runner, eagle draft-extend runner): depth **2** per runner — the WAR barrier `wait_event`s and clears `war_fastpath_read_done_event` right after `run_batch`, so at most one record is outstanding. - Scheduler `copy_done` (overlap + non-overlap spec): depth **3** — `result_queue` momentarily holds the previous result plus the just-appended one (≤2 in flight); every consumer (`batch_result_processor`, disaggregation prefill) synchronizes exactly once before a slot recurs. - **Intentionally out of scope:** the unified-memory `forward_done` event — `MultiEndedAllocator` retains and `query()`s old references, so re-recording would silently change what a retained handle reports; it needs its own lifecycle. Likewise the PP microbatch `d2h_event`s, whose lifetime is the PP async depth, not the decode pipeline. ## Test `test/registered/unit/spec/test_cuda_event_ring.py` (CI-registered): lazy fixed allocation + round-robin ordering, distinct-objects-within-depth, depth validation, and a CUDA record/wait/synchronize cycle across ring wrap-around mimicking both lifecycles. ## Benchmarks No-regression e2e posted in the comments: per-cc deltas within the harness noise band (mean +0.6%), GSM8K 0.955/0.965, AL parity. ## Checklist - signal.title: [DCP]Localize HiCache DCP indices once per transfer, not per layer
signal.text: ## Motivation Under DCP, `MLATokenToKVPoolHost.load_to_device_per_layer()` translated the widened logical slots into this rank's physical rows on every call: ```python host_indices = self.dcp_kernel_indices(host_indices) device_indices = self.dcp_kernel_indices(device_indices) ``` The result is layer-independent, but the load loop calls the method once per layer. The cost is worse than the launch count suggests. `indices[indices % dcp_size == dcp_rank]` is boolean-mask indexing, which goes through `nonzero` — and `nonzero` must read the selected count back to the host to size its output. That is a **device→host sync**, and it runs inside `with device_module.stream(self.load_stream)`, so each layer's translation blocks on the previous layer's transfer kernel. The loop serialises. `start_loading()` runs on the scheduler thread (`get_new_batch_prefill` → `ready_to_load_host_cache`), so the stall sits directly in front of the forward launch. ## Modifications - `HostKVCache.dcp_localize_indices(host_indices, device_indices)` translates a transfer's index pair once. - `load_to_device_per_layer()` now *takes* this rank's physical rows — the translation is gone from the MLA implementation. This makes explicit the precondition `_backup_from_device_per_layer` already relies on ("Indices arrive already translated…"). - `HiCacheController.start_loading()` localizes once ahead of its layer loop. - `backup_from_device_all_layer()` keeps translating internally — it owns its own layer loop, so it already paid the cost once per write-back. Not touched: the draft, HiSparse, and `HostPoolGroup` load paths. All three are rejected or non-DCP under `_resolve_hicache_dcp_compatibility`, so the translation is the identity there and un-localized indices are already correct. Pools that are not DCP-sharded return the inputs unchanged, so nothing changes unless `--dcp-size > 1`. ## Profiling Before After ## Benchmarking 8×B300, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (MLA, 27 layers), `--tp-size 8 --dcp-size 8 --page-size 64 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 4`, 16384 tokens/rank. Workload `generated-shared-prefix`: 96 groups × 4096-token prefix, 768 requests, concurrency 16 — ~3× logical KV capacity, so prefixes evict to L2 and are pulled back constantly. Both arms moved an identical **14.35M tokens** through the load path. **Scheduler-thread cost of one 27-layer load loop**, with a no-DCP run as the floor. Averaged over the complete loops in one profiler window per config (12 / 12 / 15): | | loop span | translations in loop | |---|---|---| | base | 8.99 ms | 52 | | **patched** | **1.06 ms** | **0** | | TP8, no DCP (control) | 1.02 ms | 0 | The patch lands within 4% of the no-DCP baseline. `aten::nonzero` is absent entirely from the control trace, confirming every one under DCP came from `dcp_kernel_indices`. ## Accuracy Tests No numerical change: the indices reaching the transfer kernels are identical, only computed once per transfer instead of once per layer. Two unit tests in `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hicache_dcp_host_pool.py`: the per-layer path forwards localized rows untouched, and `start_loading` localizes exactly once for all layers. The first guards a *silent* failure — re-translating at `dcp_size=8` turns 64 rows into 8 and still passes the `numel` assert inside `dcp_kernel_indices`. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Code Formatting with Pre-Commit](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-formatting-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests. - [x] Provide accuracy results. - [ ] Update documentation / docstrings / example tutorials if this PR changes the behavior of the code. - [ ] For reviewers: If you haven't made any contributions to this PR and are only assisting with merging the main branch, please remove yourself as a co-author when merging the PR. - [x] Please feel free to join our Slack channel at https://slack.sglang.ai to discuss your PR. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :x: [Run #31994533283](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994533283) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #31994532982](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994532982)

signal.title: [AMD] Avoid padded Q for unified DSV4 prefill
signal.text: ## Motivation DeepSeek V4 TP prefill currently allocates a decode-oriented 64-head padded Q tensor, then passes the local-head slice to the unified-KV attention backend. At TP=8 that slice has 16 heads and is noncontiguous, so the OPUS wrapper materializes it with `q.contiguous()` before launching the kernel. The 64-head layout is useful for the FlashMLA sparse decode specialization, but unified-KV extend/prefill does not require it. ## Modifications - reuse one unified-KV gate result within `MQALayer.forward` so layout selection and backend dispatch use the same decision (a readability change, not a measured performance source) - skip TP head padding for unified-KV extend modes and write Q directly in contiguous local-head layout - retain the existing 64-head padded layout for decode - retain existing behavior for non-unified backends - add real `MQALayer.forward` control-flow tests plus a backend-level TARGET_VERIFY routing test ## Accuracy Tests The focused suite runs through the real `MQALayer.forward` control flow and verifies: - every mode currently selected by `ForwardMode.is_extend()` uses contiguous local-head Q (EXTEND, MIXED, TARGET_VERIFY, SPLIT_PREFILL, and DLLM_EXTEND) - the unified local-head Q owns only its logical storage (`storage_nbytes == numel * element_size`), preventing a hidden 64-head backing allocation - TARGET_VERIFY enters the production unified decode route and does not call prefill - unified DECODE retains the existing 64-head padded backing layout - non-unified modes retain the previous padded behavior - active prefill-CP disables the multi-stream branch and preserves the unpadded layout The former mocked ROCm multi-stream + unified case was removed because DeepSeek-V4 disables that production combination; the HIP multi-stream helper does not implement unified-KV cache writes. Result: `5 tests passed`, `14 subtests passed` in the official ROCm MI355X image. Static validation also passed: Ruff (`F401,F821,UP037`), `py_compile`, registered-test validation, and `git diff --check`. Review also found a pre-existing nonzero-TP-rank `attn_sink` routing bug shared by both benchmark arms. It is fixed and independently reference-validated in #35092. The A/B results below remain valid as relative layout-performance evidence, while matching output tokens between two arms that shared that bug are not presented as absolute model-accuracy proof. ## Speed Tests and Profiling At the production sparse-prefill shape, the OPUS wrapper-to-kernel delta was 43.5-44.7 us per call across three runs. That delta includes wrapper dispatch and argument handling, so it is an upper bound on the removable contiguous-copy cost, not a model-level or TTFT result. ## Model E2E (MI355X, TP8 / DP1) The branch was rebased onto current `main` (`ab9e7abad`; parent `c87a2ced1`) and tested in the pinned ROCm image on 8 x MI355X. Both arms used unified-KV DSV4 attention, TP8/DP1, chunked prefill 8,192, OSL=1, distinct uncached token sequences, one warmup, and repeated scored requests. - 8K: baseline median **318.23 ms**, candidate **315.29 ms** (**0.93%** improvement); all five output tokens matched. - 64K first sandwich: baseline median **2,790.31 ms**, candidate **2,771.56 ms** (**0.68%** improvement); all five output tokens matched. Candidate had one server-side **11.90 s** outlier, so the five-sample P90/mean regressed despite the steady-state median gain. - 64K candidate follow-up: ten fresh uncached prompts, median **2,772.25 ms**, P90 **2,782.55 ms**, range **2,765.25-2,808.13 ms**, zero retractions; the outlier did not reproduce. - 64K A2/B with the same ten fresh prompt indices: baseline median/P90/mean **2,793.65 / 2,795.65 / 2,793.33 ms**; candidate **2,772.25 / 2,782.55 / 2,775.21 ms**, improving **0.77% / 0.47% / 0.65%**. All ten output tokens matched; neither arm had an outlier above 2x its median. - Baseline A1 -> A2 drift on the original five prompt indices was **0.30%** at the median (A2 slower), below the candidate's steady-state improvement. The result is a small steady-state E2E win, not the larger wrapper-level upper bound. The isolated 11.90 s event is retained as a tail-risk observation; it did not reproduce in either ten-request arm and is not attributed to this Q-layout change. ## Checklist - [x] Add focused unit tests - [x] Preserve decode and non-unified behavior - [x] Provide accuracy and operator profiling evidence - [x] Complete model E2E and graph-capture validation - [ ] Documentation update (not needed for this internal layout change) <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31995871474](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31995871474)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31995871369](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31995871369)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: [AMD] Fix DSV4 unified attention sink TP slice
signal.text: ## Motivation DeepSeek-V4 stores `attn_sink` as a global per-head parameter. The non-unified path slices it by attention-TP rank, but the unified-KV branch passed the global tensor directly. Unified prefill truncated it to the first `H` entries and unified decode indexed from head zero, so every nonzero attention-TP rank consumed rank 0's sink values. This affects pure TP configurations such as TP8/DP1. Baseline/candidate token comparisons cannot detect it when both arms share the same routing bug. ## Modifications - Pass the existing TP-local sink slice to the unified backend. - Strip the FlashMLA-only zero padding so the unified backend receives exactly `[n_local_heads]` values. - Add a real `MQALayer.forward` regression for TP8 ranks 0, 3, and 7 with distinct per-head sink values. ## Accuracy Tests The bug predates this PR: `attn_sink=self.attn_sink` entered upstream main with unified-KV support in `f2bcdb050` (#27380). It is present in this PR's base (`92b1d382c`) and was still present in upstream main `4b06f917c` when rechecked. MI355X, ROCm 7.2.26015, real DeepSeek-V4-Pro checkpoint sink (`layers.0.attn.attn_sink`), TP rank 3 / heads 48-63: - Production OPUS prefill vs independent FP32 PyTorch softmax-plus-sink reference: max abs `0.0009765625`, mean abs `5.66e-05`, passed `atol=rtol=0.02`. - Production Triton decode vs the same reference: max abs `0.001953125`, mean abs `6.20e-05`, passed `atol=rtol=0.02`. - Old rank-0 sink slice negative control: prefill max abs `0.0341796875`, decode max abs `0.0458984375`; both failed the same tolerance. Full DeepSeek-V4-Pro TP8 GSM8K (`unified_kv_triton`, FP4 experts, 1,319 questions, 8-shot, greedy, 512 max tokens, 32 clients): - Base `92b1d382c`, run 1: `1252/1319 = 94.9204%`. - Base `92b1d382c`, repeat: `1259/1319 = 95.4511%`. - Fix `3b0dfaace`: `1257/1319 = 95.2995%`. - Fix vs base run 1: `+5` questions (`+0.3791` percentage points), exact paired McNemar `p=0.424`. - Fix vs base repeat: `-2` questions (`-0.1516` percentage points), exact paired McNemar `p=0.856`. - The fix result is inside the base repeat range; therefore GSM8K establishes no regression but does **not** establish an attributable score improvement. The kernel-level reference remains the direct correctness proof. Focused tests in the official ROCm MI355X image: - Sink regression plus adjacent DeepSeek-V4 model tests: `6 passed`, `5 subtests passed`. - Ruff format/check, `py_compile`, and `git diff --check` passed. ## Checklist - [x] Add nonzero-rank TP regression coverage. - [x] Validate production prefill and decode kernels against an independent reference. - [x] Keep the production change scoped to sink routing. - [ ] Run repository CI. <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31995889269](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31995889269)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31995889181](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31995889181)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: [DSA] Trim top-k v2 output modes and tighten its PDL waits
signal.text: > Generated by Claude. ## Motivation The DeepSeek-V4 (DSA indexer) top-k v2 kernel carried an optional `raw_indices` output that no production caller ever requests: the c4 indexer routes to the v1 kernel whenever it needs raw indices, so the v2 argument was only ever exercised by a unit test. Everyone else still paid for it with a per-element `raw_out != nullptr` branch inside the page-table transform loop. While removing it, two PDL (programmatic dependent launch) details in the same kernel turned out to be leaving performance on the table or resting on a condition the caller was not told about. ## Modifications **Output modes.** `raw_indices` is gone; `page_tables` becomes optional instead. `None` selects a `TopKMode::INDICES` template that emits the selected positions straight into the output, so the transform pass -- and the 8 KB shared staging buffer it needs -- is compiled out rather than skipped at runtime. Passing a page table keeps the existing behaviour bit for bit. **Output buffer is no longer prefilled with -1.** Every path already writes all `topk` slots of every row: the collect pass fills `[0, above_count)`, `handle_tie` fills `[above_count, topk)` (padding included), and the trivial path fills everything. The per-layer fill kernel was dead work. **Level-3 PDL wait narrowed to the cluster path.** Only rows whose raw indices come from the persistent cluster kernel need that kernel to have retired. The register / streaming / trivial rows were waiting on it too, holding an SM slot until the long-running pool finished and serializing the short items behind it -- which is exactly the mix level 3 exists for. The wait now lives inside the cluster branch (block-uniform, so the following `__syncthreads()` is unaffected). **Small-batch kernel.** Dropped the redundant `PDLWaitPrimary` after `forward()` (`forward()` already waits internally) and added the missing `PDLTriggerSecondary` so dependents can be scheduled without waiting for the whole grid to drain. **PDL prefetch contract.** The kernel reads `seq_lens` and the plan metadata *before* its `griddepcontrol.wait`, which is only legal while neither is produced by the immediately preceding kernel in the stream (per CUDA: the launch trigger "provides no memory visibility guarantee itself"). Production satisfies this -- both are built during per-forward metadata prep -- but two call sites could quietly break it, so: - the DSA backend now asserts `lengths.dtype == torch.int32` instead of calling `.to(torch.int32)`, which would place a cast kernel exactly there; - the unit test no longer launches `plan_topk_v2` back to back with the transform. Also renamed `TopKMode::INDICE` to `INDICES`. ## Accuracy Tests `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_topk_v2.py` -- 234/234 pass on B200. The no-page-table mode is validated directly against `torch.topk` across every dispatch template and boundary (`test_topk_v2_output_indices`), and the paged mode is still validated by inverting the output through the page table (`test_topk_v2`, `test_topk_v2_ragged`), so both modes keep full coverage. ## Benchmarking and Profiling No kernel-algorithm change on the paged path, so throughput is unchanged for the common shapes. The wins are structural: one fewer fill kernel per layer, one fewer branch per output element in the transform loop, and short rows in a mixed-length long-context batch no longer sit blocked on the persistent cluster pool. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Code Formatting with Pre-Commit](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-formatting-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests as outlined in the [Running Unit Tests](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#running-unit-tests-adding-to-ci). <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:white_check_mark: [Run #31958299936](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31958299936)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:no_entry_sign: [Run #31958598209](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31958598209)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: fix(bcg): preserve Qwen3-VL DeepStack inputs during replay
signal.text: ## Motivation Prefill breakable CUDA graph (BCG) replay should preserve the same model semantics as eager execution. Qwen3-VL passes intermediate visual features through `input_deepstack_embeds` and adds them at selected language-model layers. However, BCG did not copy this request-specific tensor into a stable graph input slot. As a result, normal BCG execution behaved like an explicit zero-DeepStack run rather than eager execution. Requests still completed successfully, making this a silent correctness issue. ## Reproduction Environment: - Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` - Revision: `0c351dd01ed87e9c1b53cbc748cba10e6187ff3b` - GPU: NVIDIA H200 - Dtype: BF16 - Decoding: greedy, `max_new_tokens=20` - Input: deterministic RGB vertical-stripe image The GPU test harness temporarily enabled Qwen3-VL for BCG testing. The experiment compares four arms: 1. `eager_normal` 2. `eager_zero_deepstack` 3. `bcg_normal` 4. `bcg_zero_deepstack` The zero-DeepStack arms replace `input_deepstack_embeds` with zeros immediately before the language-model forward call. Each result is formatted as: ```text (common_prefix_length, all_token_ids_equal, maximum_absolute_logprob_difference) ``` | Comparison | Before fix | After fix | |---|---:|---:| | `bcg_normal` vs `eager_normal` | `(7, False, 1.154)` | `(15, True, 0.071)` | | `bcg_normal` vs `bcg_zero_deepstack` | `(20, True, 0.000)` | `(7, False, 1.148)` | | `bcg_zero_deepstack` vs `eager_zero_deepstack` | `(20, True, 0.066)` | `(20, True, 0.066)` | | `eager_zero_deepstack` vs `eager_normal` | `(7, False, 1.138)` | `unchanged` | Before the fix, `bcg_normal` was identical to `bcg_zero_deepstack` and diverged from `eager_normal`. After the fix, `bcg_normal` matches `eager_normal` at the token level and correctly diverges from `bcg_zero_deepstack`. The zero-DeepStack control remains unchanged. Instrumentation also confirmed that `input_deepstack_embeds` was present and non-zero at the language-model entry before replay. The RGB image is used only as a deterministic semantic-equivalence test, not as a visual-quality benchmark. Note on text-only numerics: the slot buffer changes the captured-graph layout, so text-only completions under BCG shift slightly relative to eager (divergence around char 78 in hardware testing, with the slot verified zero throughout). This is the same class as ordinary BCG-vs-eager drift, but anyone diffing text outputs across this PR should expect it. ## Modifications - Add an explicit `supports_bcg_deepstack_replay` capability to Qwen3-VL. - Add an optional stable `input_deepstack_embeds` buffer and graph slot. - Allocate the slot only for multimodal models that opt in and have a non-zero DeepStack width. - Pass the stable slot during BCG capture so the DeepStack additions are included in the graph. - Copy the request-specific DeepStack tensor into the slot before replay. - Clear missing and padded regions to prevent stale data from previous requests. - Fail closed when a non-empty DeepStack tensor does not fit the captured slot, instead of replaying with a zeroed slot. - Add Qwen3-VL and Qwen3-VL MoE to the breakable prefill CUDA graph allowlist. - Add unit tests for capability gating, buffer allocation, slot registration, allowlist membership, and the per-replay slot lifecycle. Absence (`None` or an empty tensor) clears the slot silently; a non-empty tensor with a mismatched shape, dtype, or device raises rather than silently downgrading the request to zero-DeepStack semantics. The `RuntimeError` fires inside the replayed forward, so if the guard ever trips it takes down the scheduler rather than failing a single request. That is the intended trade for an unreachable contract violation, where the alternative is serving a silently wrong answer. Eager fallback is not available at this site: `input_deepstack_embeds` is only materialized inside `model.forward` (via `general_mm_embed_routine` → `separate_deepstack_embeds`), already past `_prepare_forward_metadata_for_replay` and inside the replay context, so there is no pre-commit validation point. `input_embeds` cannot be reused because DeepStack has a different shape and is consumed at selected intermediate language-model layers. `supports_bcg_deepstack_replay` is inherited by every subclass of `Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration`: Qwen3.5, Qwen3.5-MoE, InternS1-Pro, InternS2-Mobius, InternS2-Preview, and the Qwen3-Omni MoE Thinker. This is deliberate. Those archs consume DeepStack through the same code path, so any checkpoint of theirs that ships non-empty `deepstack_visual_indexes` is covered without further change. Released checkpoints for those archs currently ship empty indexes, so the replay path is a no-op for them today. `MuseGlimmerForConditionalGeneration` is on the BCG allowlist but derives from a different base and does not consume DeepStack at all, so it is unaffected. Qwen3-VL and Qwen3-VL MoE now get prefill graphs by default. This changes replay-vs-eager numerics to the new baseline, and anyone who previously forced breakable prefill was silently running zero-DeepStack and should see grounding improve. ## Accuracy Tests ```bash pytest \ test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_deepstack_replay_slot.py \ test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_cuda_graph_buffer_registry.py \ test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_prefill_cuda_graph_runner.py \ test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_prefill_cuda_graph_runner_helpers.py ``` Result: ```text 55 passed, 24 warnings, 13 subtests passed in 10.70s ``` This includes 8 new tests and 47 existing adjacent tests. Allowlist membership is covered separately in `test/registered/unit/server_args/test_server_args.py`. The GPU four-arm validation results are shown in the Reproduction section. ## Speed Tests and Profiling This is a correctness fix, not a speed optimization. Models that do not activate DeepStack replay do not allocate the new buffer or perform the replay copy. For Qwen3-VL-8B with `max_num_tokens=8192`, `hidden_size=4096`, three DeepStack embeddings, and BF16, the maximum additional buffer is: ```text 8192 × 4096 × 3 × 2 bytes = 192 MiB ``` No replay-latency benchmark was performed. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [[Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests according to the [[Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [ ] Update documentation according to [[Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). No user-facing API or configuration change. - [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [[Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [[Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). Accuracy results and memory overhead are reported above; latency was not benchmarked. - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [[guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance)](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31994368293](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994368293)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:no_entry_sign: [Run #31994368080](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994368080)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: [Kernel] Add H200 GLM-4.5 fused MoE fast path
signal.text: ## Motivation Captured `zai-org/GLM-4.5-FP8` TP=8 serving traces show the per-channel FP8 fused-MoE path as a material GPU-time contributor (up to 34.9% in the highest-concurrency capture). The production layout is stable and narrow: 160 routed experts plus one fused shared expert, hidden size 5120, local intermediate size 192, and top-k 9. ## What this PR adds - Add an SM90a native-CUDA JIT kernel specialized for the captured GLM-4.5-FP8 TP=8 layout. - Fuse dynamic hidden-state FP8 quantization, expert count/sort, WGMMA GEMM1, SiLU/gate/requantization, WGMMA GEMM2, routing-weight application, and final top-k combination. - Cache TMA descriptors and a fixed-capacity per-worker workspace. - Integrate it as an opt-in fast path in the existing Triton MoE runner via `SGLANG_ENABLE_GLM45_FUSED_MOE=1`. - Add H200 correctness coverage for every token shape observed in the capture and a registered kernel benchmark. The implementation uses native CUDA C++ plus Hopper inline PTX for TMA, WGMMA, mbarrier, `cp.async`, and programmatic dependent launch. This follows the same conservative principle as prior SM90 MoE work (#8678, #16723): keep the specialized contract explicit and preserve the general backend as the fallback. ## Scope and fallback The fast path is selected only for H200, BF16 activations, FP8 E4M3 weights, FP32 per-channel scales, the exact `[E=161, H=5120, gate_up=384, intermediate=192, topk=9]` ABI, and `1 <= tokens <= 8192`. Unsupported shapes, semantic options, devices, and CUDA-graph capture remain on the existing implementation. The fixed-capacity workspace is 813,777,408 bytes per TP worker. ## H200 kernel benchmark Base commit: `92b1d382c7f4d1c82ed3a76345d6f625f1fc54a2`. Both providers run through the same `fused_experts_impl` dispatch path with CUDA graphs disabled (3 warmup, 50 replay iterations). | Captured tokens | SGLang Triton (us) | CUDA fast path (us) | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 249.536 | 44.448 | 5.614x | | 16 | 273.664 | 113.664 | 2.408x | | 64 | 200.000 | 172.192 | 1.161x | | 113 | 205.984 | 181.920 | 1.132x | | 119 | 204.832 | 181.888 | 1.126x | | 129 | 206.176 | 183.200 | 1.125x | | 1935 | 397.504 | 315.936 | 1.258x | | 3451 | 598.464 | 448.768 | 1.334x | | 7497 | 1172.576 | 878.752 | 1.334x | Geometric-mean speedup: **1.546x**. Current main has no Triton 3.6 config for this exact layout, so the baseline uses SGLang's existing Triton 3.5.1 fallback config. ## Validation - H200 JIT build: pass - H200 correctness against the SGLang Triton reference for all nine captured shapes: pass (`atol=0.10`, `rtol=0.03`) - Unsupported-shape fallback check: pass - Targeted pytest result: `10 passed` - Python compileall and new-file Ruff checks: pass - CUDA/C++ clang-format and `git diff --check`: pass ## End-to-end benchmark status The TP=8 `zai-org/GLM-4.5-FP8` main-vs-candidate serving benchmark is in progress. It will compare random and ShareGPT workloads at max concurrency 1/32/100 with approximately 1K input and 1K output tokens, reporting TTFT, TPOT, request throughput, output-token throughput, and total-token throughput. Results will be added to this draft before it is proposed for review. <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31994467741](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994467741)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31994467767](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31994467767)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: [AMD] Use native e4m3fnuz fp8 GEMM for FLUX.2 modelopt-FP8 on gfx942
signal.text: ## Motivation The FLUX.2 diffusion model shipped as a ModelOpt-FP8 checkpoint (`lmsys/flux2-dev-modelopt-fp8-sglang-transformer`) fails to serve on ROCm. The `multimodal-gen-test-2-gpu-amd` job (`test_server_2_gpu.py[flux2_modelopt_fp8_tp2_t2i]`, cluster **R192**) crashes on the first FP8 linear during warmup with: ``` RuntimeError: CUDA error: HIPBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED when calling `HIPBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED` modelopt_quant.py:425 apply -> apply_fp8_linear fp8_utils.py -> torch._scaled_mm(...) ``` **Root cause:** On ROCm **gfx942 (MI300X / MI325X)** the native fp8 dtype is **`e4m3fnuz`** (`is_fp8_fnuz()` is `True` only for `gfx94*`), so `scaled_fp8_quant()` emits **e4m3fnuz** activations. ModelOpt checkpoints (FLUX.2) ship **e4m3fn** weights. The resulting **e4m3fn (weight) × e4m3fnuz (activation)** mix makes hipBLASLt reject `torch._scaled_mm`. This is a pure format mismatch, not a numerical error, and it is **gfx942-specific**: gfx950 (MI350X/MI355X) and CUDA use native `e4m3fn`, so both operands already match there and no conversion is needed. ## Modifications **Use native fp8 (`e4m3fnuz`) matmul on gfx942 (MI300X) — no bf16 fallback.** The fix lives in `ModelOptFp8LinearMethod.process_weights_after_loading` (`python/sglang/multimodal_gen/runtime/layers/quantization/modelopt_quant.py`), which is the quant method that serves the FLUX.2 ModelOpt-FP8 checkpoint. At weight-load time, on gfx942 only (gated behind `is_fp8_fnuz()`), we: - **reinterpret the e4m3fn weights as the arch-native `e4m3fnuz`** and **double the (static) weight/input scales** via the existing `normalize_e4m3fn_to_e4m3fnuz()` helper. Because an e4m3fnuz value is half of the e4m3fn value for the same bit pattern, doubling the scale makes the dequantized result **numerically identical**. - After conversion both operands are `e4m3fnuz`, so the GEMM **stays on the native fp8 dtype through `torch._scaled_mm`** — we do **not** dequantize to bf16. This preserves the FP8 fast path and memory footprint, and makes FLUX.2 consistent with every other ROCm FP8 scheme in the codebase (which already call `normalize_e4m3fn_to_e4m3fnuz`). gfx950 / CUDA take no new path (`is_fp8_fnuz()` is `False`), so they are unaffected. The earlier dequant→bf16 fallback in `fp8_utils.py` is reverted. Net diff: `+20` lines to `modelopt_quant.py`, `0` to `fp8_utils.py`. ## Accuracy / Validation Offline-verified on real **MI300X (gfx942)** hardware (dell300x-k14-03), running the exact CI config (FLUX.2-dev base + `--transformer-path lmsys/flux2-dev-modelopt-fp8-sglang-transformer`, `--model-type diffusion --tp-size 2`): | | Stock (unpatched main) | This PR | |---|---|---| | Warmup | ❌ `HIPBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED` at `modelopt_quant.py:425` → `torch._scaled_mm` | ✅ warmup 100%, "server is fired up and ready to roll" | | Image generation | crash | ✅ `POST /v1/images/generations` → **HTTP 200** with image | | GEMM path | e4m3fn × e4m3fnuz → rejected | ✅ **native fp8** `torch._scaled_mm` (weights converted to `e4m3fnuz`) | | HIPBLAS errors | crash on warmup | **0** | Native-fp8 conversion confirmed on gfx942: `normalize_e4m3fn_to_e4m3fnuz` yields `weight.dtype == float8_e4m3fnuz`, `weight_scale ×2`, `input_scale ×2` — the GEMM stays on native fp8, not bf16. <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:white_check_mark: [Run #31989457422](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31989457422)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31989457259](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31989457259)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: feat(serving): add --enable-sort-tool-schema-keys to share prefix cache across tool key orders
signal.text: ## Motivation When different clients send semantically equivalent tool definitions with different JSON key orders (e.g., serializers that emit schema keys in different orders), the rendered prompts differ and the requests cannot share the same prefix cache, hurting prefix-cache hit rate for tool-heavy workloads. Pydantic already emits the declared fields of a tool definition (`type`, `function`, `name`, `description`, ...) in a stable order, so the free-form `function.parameters` JSON-schema payload is the only part that carries the client's key order into the rendered prompt. Normalizing it lets equivalent tool definitions map to byte-identical prompts. ### Why clients send different key orders: a real production trace This is not a hypothetical concern. In our production request trace, the same `search` tool arrived with the `properties` and `required` keys swapped between two client requests: Request A: ```json "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": {"type": "string", "description": "..."}, "time_range": {"type": "string", "description": "...", "enum": ["..."]}, "search_source": {"type": "string", "description": "...", "enum": ["..."]} }, "required": ["query", "time_range", "search_source"] } ``` Request B (same tool, different key order): ```json "parameters": { "type": "object", "required": ["query", "time_range", "search_source"], "properties": { "query": {"type": "string", "description": "..."}, "time_range": {"type": "string", "description": "...", "enum": ["..."]}, "search_source": {"type": "string", "description": "...", "enum": ["..."]} } } ``` Key order variation like this is common in practice because tool schemas are frequently built as plain dicts/maps on the client side, and the emitted order depends on the construction path: - Different client services or code paths define the same tool (e.g., one hand-writes the dict literal, another builds it via a JSON-Schema/OpenAPI generator that emits `required` at a different position). - Different languages/serializers order keys differently (e.g., Go's `encoding/json` sorts map keys alphabetically, while Python/JS preserve insertion order). - Different SDK or library versions serialize the same schema object in different field orders. Since the tool block is rendered verbatim into the prompt, requests A and B produce different token sequences at the tools section and cannot share the prefix cache, even though the tools are semantically identical. With `--enable-sort-tool-schema-keys` enabled, both render byte-identically and hit the same prefix. **Measured impact:** with our real user trace, enabling this flag increased the total prefix cache hit rate by 15 percentage points. ## Modifications - Add a new opt-in server flag `--enable-sort-tool-schema-keys` (default `False`). When enabled, the JSON-schema keys of tool parameters are recursively sorted so equivalent tool definitions share the same prefix cache. - Add `_canonicalize_tool_parameters` in `OpenAIServingChat`, applied in `_process_messages` before template rendering and constraint building. Because it normalizes the shared `Tool` objects in place, it covers every encoding path (chat template rendering, grammar/JSON-schema constraints, message-level tools, and the Responses API which routes through `ChatCompletionRequest`), keeping the grammar constraint consistent with the prompt. - Extract the existing `_sort_json` helper from `inkling_renderer.py` into a shared `sort_json` utility in `sglang.srt.utils.common` and reuse it in both places. - Document the new flag in `server_arguments.mdx`. Note: this flag is off by default and only changes the key order in which tool parameters are rendered; it does not change model behavior or request semantics. ## Accuracy Tests Tool calling accuracy was evaluated with the [Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL)](https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla/blob/main/berkeley-function-call-leaderboard/README.md), comparing the flag disabled (baseline) vs. enabled. Enabling `--enable-sort-tool-schema-keys` shows no degradation in tool calling accuracy. Baseline (flag disabled): With `--enable-sort-tool-schema-keys` enabled: ## Speed Tests and Profiling The flag is off by default and adds zero overhead when disabled. When enabled, it performs a lightweight recursive key sort on tool parameters per request (negligible compared to tokenization/inference), in exchange for a higher prefix-cache hit rate when clients send equivalent tools with differing key orders. With our real user trace, the total prefix cache hit rate increased by 15 percentage points. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed). - [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance). ## Review and Merge Process 1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process). 2. Get approvals from [CODEOWNERS](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/CODEOWNERS) and other reviewers. 3. Trigger CI tests with [comments](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#how-to-trigger-ci-tests) or contact authorized users to do so. - Common commands include `/tag-and-rerun-ci`, `/tag-run-ci-label`, `/rerun-failed-ci` 4. After green CI and required approvals, ask Merge Oncalls or people with Write permission to merge the PR. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :x: [Run #31581585839](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31581585839) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #31581585609](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31581585609)

signal.title: feat(spec): support NGRAM speculative decoding with DP attention
signal.text: ## Motivation NGRAM speculative decoding was hard-blocked when DP attention was enabled — `_handle_ngram` raised `ValueError("Currently ngram speculative decoding does not support dp attention.")`. This PR enables `--speculative-algorithm NGRAM` together with `--enable-dp-attention`. ## Modifications - **Drop the guard** in `arg_groups/speculative_hook.py`. - **`NGRAMWorker`** — handle an idle DP rank (a rank with no local requests), mirroring how EAGLE handles it: - On a global verify step — gated on the DP-gathered `is_extend_in_batch` flag (which is populated even with the overlap scheduler off, unlike `global_forward_mode`) — attach a zero-row `NgramVerifyInput` so `ForwardBatch.init_new` applies the draft-token coefficient and `global_num_tokens` scaling agrees across ranks. - Keep the idle batch in `IDLE` mode (do **not** convert it to `TARGET_VERIFY`): an idle batch stays collective-aligned through `init_new`'s idle path, which skips attention; a `bs=0` `TARGET_VERIFY` forward would instead launch the attention kernel with degenerate args. An explicit idle branch in `forward_batch_generation` runs a collective-aligned forward and returns an empty result. - **`NgramVerifyInput`** — add `create_idle_input`; expose `kv_indptr`/`kv_indices` as `None` so the decode/idle attention-metadata path builds plain metadata from `seq_lens`. (`num_tokens_per_req` is no longer part of this PR — #31013 landed it upstream.) - **`forward_batch_info`** — NGRAM captures no hidden states, so an idle DP rank carrying a zero-row `NgramVerifyInput` reaches the extend/idle slice with `hidden_states` `None`; guard it. This mirrors the identical guard #33537 added on the sibling `target_verify` branch of the same function. - **Tests** — unit test for the guard removal; e2e GSM8K test (tp2/dp2). ## Accuracy Tests Validated on 2× H20. GSM8K (200q / 5-shot / temp 0) parity vs the dp-on **non-spec** baseline: | backend | baseline-dp | ngram-dp | |---|---|---| | triton | 0.930 | 0.930 | | flashinfer (1000q) | 0.914 | 0.915 | At 1000 questions on flashinfer, correctness flips are balanced (C→W = 7 / W→C = 8, McNemar p ≈ 1.0) — i.e. lossless up to floating-point. dp-off regression (NGRAM without DP): 0.935. The new e2e test passes on a Qwen3-30B-A3B-class target: GSM8K 0.935. ## Speed Tests and Profiling NGRAM acceptance length is ~10 on repetitive workloads and is unaffected by DP (dp-triton 10.65, no-dp-triton 12.43, dp-flashinfer 10.65) — DP attention does not degrade speculation. On GSM8K (math reasoning, less repetitive) accept length is ~1.8. ## Note: pre-existing DP issue with `qwen2.py` models (out of scope) The default NGRAM CI target (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, `qwen2.py`) has an **unrelated, pre-existing** DP-attention bug that reproduces with **no speculative decoding**: under `--enable-dp-attention` the attention emits KV heads split by `tp_size` while the DP KV pool holds the full head count, so the KV store fails (`view` / `store_cache` mismatch) at warmup. The e2e test therefore uses the DP-attention-capable `Qwen3-30B-A3B` target (the same model as the EAGLE DP test). Filed separately as #28615. ## Checklist - [x] Format code with pre-commit (black / isort / ruff) - [x] Add unit tests (guard removal) and an e2e test (GSM8K, tp2/dp2) - [x] Provide accuracy and speed results (above) - [x] Follow the SGLang code style guidance <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31993220750](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31993220750)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31993220668](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31993220668)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->

signal.title: [Bug] Prometheus /metrics scrape can starve prefill bootstrap health checks
signal.text: ### Checklist - [x] I searched related issues but found no solution. - [x] The bug persists in the latest version. - [x] This is a bug report, not a general question. - [x] This issue is written in English. ### Describe the bug I observed the following failure pattern in a PD deployment: - `/metrics` latency on the prefill leader suddenly increased to seconds. - The bootstrap `/health` endpoint started returning read timeouts, even though the handler itself only returns `OK`. - Decode workers reported `Losing connection with prefill instance` for the same prefill bootstrap address. - After `/metrics` pressure stopped, `/health` became fast again. This makes the prefill instance look disconnected even when the process is still alive. The symptom is a false prefill connection loss caused by health-check starvation. After reading the code, I think the problem is in the current `/metrics` serving path: - In single-tokenizer prefill mode, `TokenizerManager` owns both the HTTP server that exposes `/metrics` and the bootstrap health server used by decode heartbeats. - `add_prometheus_middleware()` mounts the Prometheus ASGI app directly on the main app with `CollectorRegistry`, `MultiProcessCollector`, and `make_asgi_app`. - Each scrape can read and aggregate Prometheus multiprocess files and generate the full text response in the request path. - Concurrent scrapes can enter this path at the same time. - When this collection path becomes slow, it shares the same Python process failure domain as bootstrap health handling, so `/health` can be starved. I tested a small experimental patch to compare behavior. Patch approach: - Run metrics collection in a subprocess so it is isolated from the main event loop. - Apply singleflight: at most one scrape generates metrics at a time; concurrent scrapes are rejected immediately. - Enforce a bounded timeout on generation so a slow collection cannot block the server indefinitely. Prototype diff (single commit, hash-pinned): - https://github.com/junliu-mde/sglang/commit/c31b7ca2283b557cf4b5d9e9c979f52e58954c70 The comparison result was straightforward: - Before the patch, local `/metrics` scrape pressure caused bootstrap health misses and decode-side `Losing connection with prefill instance` logs. - After the patch, a stronger `/metrics` scrape test produced no health misses. Extra concurrent scrapes failed fast instead of piling up behind metrics generation. This patch is not intended as the final design. It only validates that isolating, bounding, and limiting `/metrics` generation protects the critical health path. In principle, returning `503` immediately for concurrent scrapes is already enough to mitigate the starvation: each rejected scrape exits quickly instead of blocking, so `/health` is no longer crowded out. For a production design, however, the preferred fix should still be code-path isolation: metrics exposition should not share the same Python failure domain as critical health or heartbeat handling. Prometheus exporter guidance also points in this direction. It says exporters should normally pull metrics synchronously when Prometheus scrapes them, and that caching is acceptable only for particularly expensive metrics and should be called out in the metric `HELP` string. The same guidance notes that the default Prometheus scrape timeout is 10 seconds, so any bounded generation timeout should stay below the configured scrape timeout. See: https://prometheus.io/docs/instrumenting/writing_exporters/#scheduling A bounded cache of the last successful Prometheus metrics snapshot can still be useful, but it should be treated as a secondary protection rather than the primary fix. Serving cached bytes to concurrent scrapes can keep the `/metrics` HTTP path constant-time under scrape pressure and preserve Prometheus data continuity, but stale data must be bounded, documented, and observable. `503`/`504` should still surface when there is genuinely no usable snapshot, when the snapshot is too stale, or when generation repeatedly fails. ### Reproduction Run a PD deployment where the prefill leader uses the single-tokenizer topology and metrics are enabled. From the affected prefill pod, apply local scrape pressure to `/metrics` while probing bootstrap health. Example procedure: 1. Start multiple local clients scraping `http://127.0.0.1:30000/metrics`. 2. In parallel, probe `http://127.0.0.1:8998/health` with a short read timeout. 3. Watch decode logs for `Losing connection with prefill instance`. 4. Stop the `/metrics` pressure and verify that `/health` becomes fast again. ### Environment `python3 -m sglang.check_env` on the affected prefill pod: ``` Python: 3.12.3 (main, Mar 23 2026, 19:04:32) [GCC 13.3.0] CUDA available: True GPU 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPU 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 Compute Capability: 9.0 CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 13.0, V13.0.88 CUDA Driver Version: 590.48.01 PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130 sglang: 0.5.12 sglang-kernel: 0.4.2.post2 flashinfer_python: 0.6.11.post1 flashinfer_cubin: 0.6.11.post1 flashinfer_jit_cache: 0.6.11.post1+cu130 triton: 3.6.0 transformers: 5.6.0 torchao: 0.17.0+cu130 numpy: 2.3.5 aiohttp: 3.13.5 fastapi: 0.136.1 huggingface_hub: 1.15.0 orjson: 3.11.9 outlines: 0.1.11 pydantic: 2.13.4 pyzmq: 27.1.0 uvicorn: 0.47.0 uvloop: 0.22.1 xgrammar: 0.2.0 ulimit soft: 1048576 ```

signal.title: [DCP] Build the MHA-extend reorg offsets on the host
signal.text: ## Motivation `all_gather_kv_cache_for_mha_extend` builds its two cumulative-length tensors on the **device**, then uses them as Python slice bounds: ```python prefix_lens_cu = torch.zeros(len(seq_lens) + 1, dtype=torch.int32, device=kv_a.device) extend_lens_cu = torch.zeros_like(prefix_lens_cu) prefix_lens_cu[1:] = torch.cumsum(extend_prefix_lens, dim=0) extend_lens_cu[1:] = torch.cumsum(extend_seq_lens, dim=0) for i in range(len(seq_lens)): kv_a_tuple += (prefix_kv_a[prefix_lens_cu[i] : prefix_lens_cu[i+1]], kv_a[extend_lens_cu[i] : extend_lens_cu[i+1]]) k_pe_tuple += (prefix_k_pe[prefix_lens_cu[i] : prefix_lens_cu[i+1]], k_pe[extend_lens_cu[i] : extend_lens_cu[i+1]]) ``` Each bound goes through `__index__` → `.item()` → a **device→host sync**: 8 per request, per call. This runs inside the forward on the scheduler thread, so the CPU cannot run ahead and batch prep stops overlapping GPU work. Profiled on 8×B300 with DCP8, this was **27,982 `aten::item` calls costing 430 ms in a 6.7 s window**, plus 14,878 `cudaStreamSynchronize`. The same profile of a `--tp-size 8` run with no DCP shows 243 stream syncs total. The sibling `all_gather_kv_cache_for_dcp` already builds its offsets on the host and does not have this problem. ## Modifications The host-side lengths already exist — the function is handed `extend_prefix_lens_cpu`, and `ForwardBatch` carries `extend_seq_lens_cpu` right beside it (`forward_batch_info.py:535-536`, set together). Accumulate both on the host with `itertools.accumulate` and slice with plain ints. `extend_prefix_lens` / `extend_seq_lens` are then unused, and `seq_lens` was only supplying a length, so all three drop out of the signature. Both call sites updated (`forward_mha.py`, `forward_mha_rocm.py`). ## Accuracy Tests Greedy decode over a shared prefix reused by four queries of differing extend lengths — the exact path this function reorganizes. Output digest is **identical** before and after (`752a08531231e97a`), so the reorg is unchanged. `test/registered/dcp/test_dsv31_dcp8_gsm8k.py` covers this path in CI. ## Benchmarking and Profiling 8×B300, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (MLA, 27 layers), `--tp-size 8 --dcp-size 8 --page-size 64`, shared-prefix workload (96 groups × 4096-token prefix, 768 requests, concurrency 16). | | before | after | |---|---|---| | `aten::item` | 27,982 / 430.4 ms | 13,152 / **20.3 ms** | | `cudaStreamSynchronize` | 14,878 / 307.7 ms | 832 / **16.5 ms** | | `all_gather_kv_cache_for_mha_extend` | 4.35 ms/call | **2.05 ms/call** | | `run_batch` | 22.4 ms/call | **17.9 ms/call** | Stream syncs drop **94%**, landing near the 243 of a no-DCP run. The remaining `.item()` calls are on CPU tensors in `all_gather_kv_cache_for_dcp` and cost 20 ms rather than 430 ms. End to end (fresh server per arm, 2 reps, no profiler): median TTFT **−15.0%** (451.8 → 384.1 ms), mean TTFT −7.6% (465.2 → 430.0 ms), throughput +1.0%. The workload is concurrency-bound, so latency moves more than throughput. ## Checklist - [x] Format your code according to the [Code Formatting with Pre-Commit](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-formatting-with-pre-commit). - [x] Provide accuracy results. - [ ] Add unit tests — the sync is only observable on a live CUDA + DCP process group; suggestions for a cheap guard welcome. - [ ] Update documentation / docstrings / example tutorials if this PR changes the behavior of the code. - [ ] For reviewers: If you haven't made any contributions to this PR and are only assisting with merging the main branch, please remove yourself as a co-author when merging the PR. - [x] Please feel free to join our Slack channel at https://slack.sglang.ai to discuss your PR. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- pr-states:start --> --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): <!-- slot:pr-test:start -->:x: [Run #31865166090](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31865166090)<!-- slot:pr-test:end --> Latest PR Test (Extra): <!-- slot:pr-test-extra:start -->:x: [Run #31865167030](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/31865167030)<!-- slot:pr-test-extra:end --> <!-- pr-states:end -->
